title: No Blame on Lovers
intro: A poem in praise of the Prophet by the contemporary Jordanian poet Ihab al-Shabatat, in the mutaqarib metre. It opens with a love prelude, as praise poems for the Prophet traditionally do: the poet excuses lovers, describes a woman walking through the night like a sun so bright the moon goes dark for her, and an eye that shoots him after a greeting of peace. He has repented of every sin but one love, his love for “Hamza's nephew”, and with that the poem turns to praise: the Prophet's mission of truth, his courage and his forgiveness, the hearts he won without a weapon, his birth, which was mankind's cure, and his death, which left it scattered homes with their lamps gone out. The poet then apologises that words fall short of him, praises the clear white road he left behind and the Companions who drove back the darkness with swords and with books, and closes with a greeting of peace. It sets modern images in the old form, such as a vaccine that cures a patient given up for lost and water beading on a surface. An explanation of each line was published with the recording.

translation: No blame, none, on lovers,
whether they keep their love secret or reveal it.
1.sharh: There is no blame on lovers, whether they hide their love or show it. The poem opens, as praise poems for the Prophet often do, with a love prelude, and its first word excuses the love it will end by giving to the Prophet.

translation: The tongue keeps the secret, but how can the eyes
be turned away when the beloved's phantom passes?
2.sharh: Eyes give away what the tongue keeps hidden.

translation: She swayed before me through a pitch-dark night,
and the moon's eclipse above me was her doing,
3.sharh: The moon has gone dark because her beauty outshone it, leaving no light in the night but hers.

translation: so that I might see a sun adorned by night,
as if the nights were a sash on a neck.
4.sharh: The darkness around her sets her off as a jewelled sash sets off a neck.

translation: She had the scent of roses beaded with dew,
and a morning came a little before the morning.
5.sharh: Roses carry dew in the early morning, so her scent brings a dawn before the dawn.

translation: She walks unhurried in the calm of evening,
and in my heart the winds of longing storm.
6.sharh: Her slow, quiet walk is set against the storm in his heart.

translation: A hand greeted me, and an eye shot at me:
after a greeting of peace, is my blood made lawful?
7.sharh: A greeting of peace was a promise of safety; her hand gives it and her eye breaks it.

translation: It is as if the eyes of beautiful women were a sanctuary,
well guarded, round which spears are hurled.
8.sharh: Every glance of those eyes is a spear that keeps the lover off.

translation: I have been struck by every affliction, but no
wound has stayed with me like the wound of love.
9.sharh: Of all wounds, love's lasts longest.

translation: I have sinned most sins, and repented,
but there is no leave to repent of love.
10.sharh: He has repented of every sin but love; the next line says which love.

translation: As for my love of Hamza's nephew,
to abide in it is salvation.
11.sharh: Calling the Prophet “Hamza's nephew” recalls his noble line and his uncle Hamza, the lord of martyrs. This is the love he will never repent of, and here the love prelude turns to praise.

translation: Leave me with my sorrow, for my eyelids
are a cloud whose rain is too scant for it.
12.sharh: His longing for the Prophet is greater than any tears can answer.

translation: The parting of those who left has wet my eyes,
and burned my poor heart when they waved farewell.
13.sharh: The parting of those who left brought tears to his eyes and heat to his liver as they waved goodbye. For the Arabs the liver, like the heart, was the seat of grief, and the diminutive makes it tender.

translation: Whenever I remember a caravan that has gone,
the Chosen One appears to me before all who left in it:
14.sharh: Every parting reminds him first of the parting from the Prophet.

translation: a Messenger from God who went forth with the truth,
and falsehood was struck lame by him;
15.sharh: The Messenger went forth with the truth, and every falsehood he met was struck lame: after him it could not stand.

translation: free of every fault, bold in war,
and yet the end of his victories was forgiveness.
16.sharh: Fearless in battle and forgiving in victory: every triumph ended in pardon.

translation: He humbled tyrants with a sword, and won
hearts with no weapon in his hands.
17.sharh: Force for tyrants, mercy for hearts.

translation: Whenever truth bled, I thought
it was the blood of his heart and tongue that was shed.
18.sharh: The “two smallest parts” of a man, his heart and tongue, were his only weapons for winning hearts; when truth is wounded, it is as if they bleed.

translation: May I be the ransom of the hearts that were touched
by the fire-sticks of truth that struck fire in them.
19.sharh: Fire was made by working an upper stick against a lower one. The Prophet's call is the upper, the heart the lower, and light comes from their meeting, not from either alone.

translation: It was as if, soon after his birth, we were
a patient the doctors had given up, cured by a vaccine;
20.sharh: Mankind is one patient past hope, and his birth the cure; the vaccine is a modern image in the old form.

translation: and as if, soon after his death, we were
homes that lamplight has fled for good.
21.sharh: After his death mankind is no longer one body but scattered homes, each with its lamp gone out.

translation: How often a cloud above him burned with envy
when it saw that the plains had cooled his shoes.
22.sharh: The sky envies the earth for the touch of his feet, and its cloud grows hot with jealousy.

translation: He was of humankind, but its pure essence:
some of what is in the bee is pure honey.
23.sharh: He was human, but the best of humankind, as some of what comes from the bee is pure honey (Quran 16:69). The line borrows al-Mutanabbi's “musk is part of the gazelle's blood”.

translation: Prophet of guidance, the love of you is in my heart,
and human tongues are not wide enough for it.
24.sharh: No words can hold what the heart feels.

translation: Forgive the daughters of my tongue when
they reach you, and they are ugly:
25.sharh: He asks the Prophet's pardon for his words, which fall short of him: what his tongue gives birth to is not fine enough for the one it praises.

translation: the eloquence of the two revelations has risen so high in beauty
that, beside such beauty, the fair have grown ugly.
26.sharh: The two revelations are the Quran and the Sunna; beside their eloquence any fine speech looks plain.

translation: You left us a white road
on which the dark of night is as clear as day,
27.sharh: A hadith says: “I have left you on a white road whose night is like its day.”

translation: a white road, which praise cannot embroider,
but those who walk it have shining faces;
28.sharh: Nothing can be embroidered on pure white, so praise adds nothing to the road; its beauty shows in the faces of those who travel it.

translation: just as its colours neither adorn a cloud nor mar it:
while its rains pour heavy.
29.sharh: A cloud is judged by its rain, not its colours, and the Prophet's way by its fruits, not by its praisers.

translation: Were it not for the blackness that rules the hearts,
true things would never have been missed by the eyes.
30.sharh: The fault is in the heart, not the eye (Quran 22:46): a hadith says each sin leaves a black spot on the heart, until the stain covers it. The black of sinful hearts is set against the white road of lines 27 and 28.

translation: You reached the brightest light of truth,
a sun granted through the turning of night and day.
31.sharh: He is a sun that does not set at night but shines on through every turn of night and day.

translation: You lived on though lost to us, and your guidance
still sheds its scent through the passing ages.
32.sharh: From the turning of days in the line before, the poem rises to the turning of ages: his guidance outlives him.

translation: Is not the modesty on the God-fearing
your dew, beading on their faces?
33.sharh: The modesty on the faces of the God-fearing is his generosity, condensing there like dew: nada means both dew and generosity. The poem again takes a modern sense for an old word, as with the vaccine of line 20.

translation: Your hands softened hard souls,
and the bit went gentle and the bolting ceased.
34.sharh: Souls are bolting horses, and his guidance the bit that gentles them.

translation: The bridle of guidance turned hearts back,
and the gain was ours, not against us.
35.sharh: The race is against Satan, and the bridle of guidance wins it for us.

translation: The footsteps of the prophets, and the Companions' steps upon them,
are lighthouses in the night, dressed in shining white.
36.sharh: The prophets' footsteps, with the Companions' steps following in them, light the night of ignorance.

translation: Your Companions are first to be remembered when
a friend arrives, or parting calls him away.
37.sharh: Every meeting and parting reminds him first of the Companions, as every departing caravan brought the Prophet to mind in line 14.

translation: They are the arrows in the bow of the best of mankind;
the hand of God shoots, and goodness is won.
38.sharh: The Companions are arrows, the Prophet the bow, God the archer, and through them goodness was won. An allusion to the Quran (8:17): “You did not throw when you threw, but God threw.”

translation: With white swords and black texts
they swept the darkness from East and West.
39.sharh: White swords and black ink: they opened the world with arms and with learning.

translation: The peace of the One who is Peace be on the Chosen One,
and may peace come to us as well.
40.sharh: The poem ends with God's peace on the Prophet and a hope that peace may reach the poet and his hearers too. Since al-Salam is one of God's names, “the peace of Peace” is God's own peace.

3.2.4.meaning: Janah: literally “wing”, also “hand”; she has a hand in it.

4.2.4.meaning: Wishah: a broad jewelled sash worn across the shoulder.

5.2.2.meaning: Qubayla: a little before; diminutive of qabla.

8.1.3.head: غانِيَة
8.1.3.meaning: Ghawani: beautiful women; plural of ghaniya, one who needs no adornment.

8.1.4.head: حِمى
8.1.4.meaning: Hima: a protected ground no one may enter.

11.1.3-5.meaning: Ibn akhi Hamza: “Hamza's nephew”, the Prophet. Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, his uncle, was also his foster-brother.

13.2.2.head: كُبَيد
13.2.2.meaning: Kubayd: “little liver”, a tender diminutive of kabid.

18.2.3.head: الأَصغَران
18.2.3.meaning: Al-asgharan: “the two smallest parts” of a man, his heart and tongue.

19.2.1.head: زَند
19.2.1.meaning: Zinad: fire-sticks; the upper stick that is worked against the lower to make fire.

20.2.4.meaning: Liqah: a vaccine, which gives the body immunity or treats a disease.

23.1.4.head: نُقاوَة
23.1.4.meaning: Nuqawa: the choicest part, the pure essence.

25.1.3-4.meaning: Banat lisani: “the daughters of my tongue”, my words.

26.1.2.head: الوَحيان
26.1.2.meaning: Al-wahyan: “the two revelations”, the Quran and the Sunna.

27.1.1-2.meaning: Bayda': “the white”, the clear road the Prophet left; subul are roads.

29.2.3.meaning: Sihah: heavy, full of water; properly said of fat sheep.

30.1.3.head: سادَ
30.1.3.meaning: Yasudu: rules over; it plays on sawad, “blackness”.

31.2.2.head: الجَديدان
31.2.2.meaning: Al-jadidan: “the two ever-new ones”, night and day.

32.2.4.head: أَفاحَ
32.2.4.meaning: Yufah: is poured out, with a hint of faha, “to spread”, said of perfume.

33.2.5.meaning: Irtishah: in its modern sense, vapour condensing in beads on a surface.

34.2.2.head: شَكيمَة
34.2.2.meaning: Shakim: the bit across a horse's mouth.

36.2.1.head: مَنارَة
36.2.1.meaning: Mana'ir: towers with a light at the top to guide the way; lighthouses.

37.2.5.meaning: Barah: departure, parting; or open country, calling a man to travel.

39.2.3.head: المَشرِقان
39.2.3.meaning: Al-mashriqan: “the two Easts”, East and West.

40.1.2.meaning: Al-Salam: “Peace”, one of the names of God.

40.2.1.head: عَلَّ
40.2.1.meaning: Alla: perhaps; a form of la'alla.
